name: Wadandi Track
reason: Rule 1: the Shire of Augusta Margaret River (managing authority) trail page names it: a walk/cycle rail trail on the former Busselton–Flinders Bay railway, 46 km open in two sections (Busselton Jetty–Carbunup River, Cowaramup–Sebbes Road), being completed to 109 km by 2028. Rule 2 met (walk or ride it).
objection: Only one counted source and that is a council page, not a tourism or guide listing; the trail is incomplete until 2028 and the note placed it 'around Augusta', whereas the open sections are Busselton and Cowaramup; may be better added once finished. Case for: state-funded flagship trail the region is promoting.

name: Boranup Forest
reason: Rules 1-3: Australia's South West board listing plus the DBCA Leeuwin-Naturaliste page for Boranup Forest (Boranup Drive through westernmost karri forest, Boranup Lookout, campground, picnic area); a distinct forest drive and lookout off Caves Road, free entry.
objection: It is part of Leeuwin-Naturaliste National Park; if the park itself is a spot the forest could read as a sub-part. But the guides treat it as its own named stop.

name: Gloucester Tree
reason: Rules 1-2: Wikivoyage Pemberton (Do: 'maybe the most popular' lookout tree) and DBCA's Gloucester Tree page; a 1947 fire-lookout karri with climbing pegs to a 37 m (lookout) platform, plus picnic area and forest walks. Obvious draw, 8,442 page views.
objection: DBCA notes a South West Climbing Trees Project to upgrade platforms and reopen the trees to climbing, so climbing may be intermittently closed; the tree, walks and picnic area remain open whatever.

name: Diamond Tree
reason: Rule 2: DBCA says the Diamond Tree is 'now permanently CLOSED for climbing' (rot in the base, 2019); what is left is a picnic area and short walk at a roadside tree. Its draw (climbing) is closed and Wikivoyage's listing is out of date.
objection: Still a historic 1940 lookout tree with a picnic stop and walk, 2,500 page views; could be a 15-minute roadside look. Not a distinct draw once the climb is gone.

name: Beedelup Falls
reason: Rules 1-3: Wikivoyage Pemberton (See) and Australia's South West board listing, and DBCA's Greater Beedelup NP page ('Don't miss Beedelup Falls'): falls, boardwalk and suspension bridge, the Walk-Through Tree on the 4.5 km loop.
objection: Falls are seasonal (best in winter and spring) and the boardwalk area is a short visit; but two counted sources and the loop walk make it a full stop.

name: Pemberton Tramway
reason: A spot is a place, not the way you get there: the Pemberton Tramway Company is an operator's tram ride; the karri forest it runs through is covered by Gloucester Tree / Warren National Park.
objection: Wikivoyage and the board list it, and a heritage tram could be 'the ride is the attraction' (COVERAGE exception); but it runs to the Warren River bridge forest, not a distinct named place, and the forest is listed separately. Mention in the Pemberton description or a spot bio.

name: Karri Forest Explorer
reason: Rule 3: an 86 km drive route that links places judged on their own (Gloucester Tree, Beedelup Falls, Warren National Park and its Bicentennial Tree); it is the way between those spots, not a distinct place.
objection: DBCA promotes it as a named touring drive and visitors do plan around it; the owner may prefer it as a route spot. Its content is already carried by the parks and trees it links.

name: Heartbreak Trail
reason: Rule 3: a one-way drive inside Warren National Park (DBCA Warren page: 'drive the Heartbreak Trail or the Karri Forest Explorer'); part of a larger spot.
objection: It is the park's signature drive down to the Warren River; if Warren National Park were rejected it would be the place to keep instead.

name: Great Forest Trees Drive
reason: Rule 3: the 50 km drive is part of Shannon National Park (DBCA Shannon page), which is kept as the spot; the drive goes in its bio.
objection: It is the main thing visitors do in Shannon; an owner could prefer the drive's name over the park's.

name: Snake Gully Lookout
reason: Rule 3: a lookout inside Shannon National Park (DBCA names it with Big Tree Grove as a top spot in the park); part of a larger spot, kept via the park.
objection: DBCA singles it out by name; could be a sub-spot if the park ends up a destination of its own.

name: Big Tree Grove
reason: Rule 3: a grove on a walk inside Shannon National Park; part of the park, kept via Shannon National Park. (Its Wikipedia title is a California grove, so it also lacks a stable reference.)
objection: DBCA names it as one of the best places to see 90 m karri; could be a sub-spot of a Shannon destination.

name: King Jarrah Heritage Trail
reason: Rules 1-2: DBCA 'King Jarrah' park page and Trails WA (state trails site): a 45 m, roughly 500-year-old jarrah saved from sleeper cutters, with a 600 m sealed path, picnic area and BBQs, 4.5 km from Manjimup; free. Second-tier stop two counted sources name. Name it 'King Jarrah' (the sources' name); there is no Wikipedia article at this title, and a different 'King Jarrah Heritage Trail' exists in Lane Poole Reserve near Dwellingup (Peel, closed after fire), so do not take coordinates or photos from that one.
objection: Short visit (about 30 min) at a single tree on the edge of town; arguably a local picnic reserve.

name: Shannon National Park
reason: Rules 1-3: DBCA Shannon NP page: old-growth karri, the 50 km Great Forest Trees Drive, Snake Gully Lookout, Big Tree Grove, Mokare's Rock boardwalk, Shannon Dam walk, campground and horse camp. Visitor source names plenty to do; holds the drive, lookout and grove candidates.
objection: Only one counted source (the agency's own page) and 706 views; a quieter park than Warren or Gloucester.

name: Warren National Park
reason: Rules 1-3: DBCA Warren NP page and Wikivoyage Pemberton (Dave Evans Bicentennial Tree, 'excellent campgrounds'): karri forest, the Bicentennial Tree climb, Heartbreak Trail drive, Warren River canoeing and two campgrounds.
objection: The Dave Evans Bicentennial Tree is its headline; if the tree is listed separately, the park could be a near-duplicate. The Bicentennial Tree is not in this shard, so the park carries it here.

name: Greater Beedelup National Park
reason: Rule 3: duplicate of Beedelup Falls: DBCA's park page is about the falls, the Walk-Through Tree and the loop walk between them, which the Beedelup Falls spot covers.
objection: The park has its own DBCA page and the Karri Forest Explorer passes through; owner could prefer the park name with the falls as its bio.

name: Gloucester National Park
reason: DBCA page: karri forest walks (Gloucester Tree–Cascades 12 km, 10 km loop, Pemberton town link), mountain biking, the Cascades rapids on Lefroy Brook, Aerial Adventure Pemberton. More than the tree alone.
objection: Near-duplicate of the Gloucester Tree, which is what visitors come for and which sits in it; one counted source (the agency's own page). Keep only if the Cascades/trails are not carried by the tree spot.

name: Blackwood River National Park
reason: DBCA page: canoeing, swimming and fishing on WA's longest continuously flowing river, Sues Bridge and Chapman Pool day-use areas and campgrounds; free entry. The board also lists 'Blackwood River'.
objection: One counted source; the park is a string of river campgrounds rather than a single draw, and paddling the Blackwood is equally done from Nannup or Augusta; may be better as 'Blackwood River' with its access point.

name: Yelverton National Park
reason: Rules 1-2: DBCA's page lists no visitor facilities, walks or sites, only rare-flora protection; no source names anything to see or do.
objection: Native forest near Margaret River, 350 views; the Wadandi Track skirts it, but that is a separate candidate.

name: Wellington National Park
reason: Rules 1-3: DBCA page and Australia's South West board listing: Collie River valley, Wellington Dam mural, Honeymoon Pool, Potters Gorge, Wambenger mountain-bike trails, kayak and walk trails, campgrounds, kiosk. Two counted sources.
objection: Holds Wellington Dam and Honeymoon Pool, which are judged separately; risk of three overlapping spots. A clear park in its own right.

name: Wellington Dam
reason: Rules 1-3: DBCA Wellington NP page ('the largest dam mural painting in the world', by Guido van Helten; a lookout to view it; kiosk) and Australia's South West board listing. A distinct draw within the park.
objection: Lies inside Wellington National Park, also kept; could be folded into the park's bio. The mural makes it a named sight in its own right.

name: Honeymoon Pool
reason: Rules 1-3: DBCA site page (swimming, canoeing, picnic area, viewing platform over the Collie River, three campgrounds; Jabitj Trail to the dam) and Australia's South West board listing. Two counted sources.
objection: Inside Wellington National Park, about 10 km from Wellington Dam; a third Wellington spot could be thin. Swimming and camping make it a distinct stop.

name: Mount Frankland National Park
reason: Outside the region: belongs to wa-great-southern (Walpole Wilderness, reached from Walpole; wa-regions.md puts Walpole and its parks in Great Southern, and that region's candidate list already has Mount Frankland National Park).
objection: On the merits it would keep (DBCA page: granite summit lookout, Caldyanup and Summit trails). It lies in the Shire of Manjimup, the South West administrative region, so the proposer must make sure Great Southern does keep it.

name: D'Entrecasteaux National Park
reason: Rules 1-3: Australia's South West board listing and DBCA's park page: 130 km of wild coast between Augusta and Walpole, Yeagarup Dunes, Point D'Entrecasteaux and The Window, Black Point basalt columns, Windy Harbour, Mount Chudalup, Lake Jasper. Obvious draw.
objection: Huge linear park, much of it 4WD-only; it needs a single visitor point (Point D'Entrecasteaux/Windy Harbour) and the eastern end (Mandalay Beach) is Great Southern.

name: Yeagarup Dunes
reason: Rules 1-3: Australia's South West board listing and DBCA's D'Entrecasteaux page (boardwalk over Yeagarup Lake, 'traverse the mighty Yeagarup Dunes by four-wheel drive'; the largest land-locked mobile dune system in the southern hemisphere). A distinct named draw.
objection: Inside D'Entrecasteaux National Park (also kept), and the dunes proper need a 4WD; a 2WD visitor sees only the lake boardwalk at the dunes' edge.

name: Dalgarup National Park
reason: Rule 1: no counted visitor source found (no DBCA site page, no Wikivoyage or board listing); only Wikipedia and AllTrails.
objection: 330 views; AllTrails lists a jarrah-forest walk near Bridgetown.

name: Whicher National Park
reason: Rule 1: no counted visitor source found (no DBCA site page, no board or Wikivoyage listing); only Wikipedia and a 2016 wildflower-society post.
objection: 496 views; a forest park on the Whicher Range near Busselton that wildflower walkers use.

name: Lake Muir National Park
reason: The candidate park has no DBCA page, but the visitor point beside it does: DBCA's Lake Muir Observatory page (110 m boardwalk through the wetlands to a raised bird hide, picnic shelter, toilets; 'a popular rest stop on the Muir Highway'), also listed by Southern Forests and Valleys. If added, name it Lake Muir Observatory (it is in Lake Muir Nature Reserve, just north of the national park).
objection: A highway rest stop with a 15-30 minute boardwalk; the lake can be a dry bed in summer. Only the agency page plus a local tourism listing.

name: Black Diamond Pool
reason: Rules 1-3: Wikivoyage Collie (See: abandoned coal mine lake, vivid blue-green, swimming) and Australia's South West board listing (Black Diamond Lake). Two counted sources; a known swimming stop. Use the board's name, Black Diamond Lake.
objection: Shire signs warn of low pH and bacteria (naegleria traces) and it has had a drowning; swimming is at your own risk. Not closed per any source found.

name: Harris Dam
reason: Wikivoyage Collie (See): picnic lawns below the dam wall and a walk trail to the top for the view.
objection: One counted source; Wikivoyage itself says 'look is all you can do' (no water activities): a picnic area by a water-supply dam, mostly local use.

name: Glen Mervyn Dam
reason: Wikivoyage Collie (See): a crescent-shaped dam for water skiing, boating and camping, with a bushland walk.
objection: One counted source; a local boating and camping reservoir that visitors from elsewhere rarely travel for.

name: Minninup Pool
reason: Wikivoyage Collie (See): a wide section of the Collie River 3 km south of town for swimming and canoeing; the Shire tests its water with Black Diamond and Stockton.
objection: One counted source; a local swimming hole, and Collie already has stronger swimming spots (Black Diamond, Stockton Lake, Honeymoon Pool).

name: Stockton Lake
reason: Rules 1-3: Wikivoyage Collie (See: old coal-mine lake with white chalky cliffs, swimming, water skiing, camping, the 1926 mine entrance) and Australia's South West board listing. Two counted sources.
objection: A near-twin of Black Diamond Pool 10 km away (both former mine lakes for swimming); the owner may want only one.

name: Swinging Bridge Collie
reason: Rule 3: a minor suspension footbridge in town; Wikivoyage presents it as a short treat for kids, a few minutes' look, and it is a point on the Collie River Walk.
objection: Named in Wikivoyage's See list.

name: Collie River Walk
reason: Wikivoyage Collie (Do/Hike): a 9 km walk following the Collie River through town.
objection: One line in one source; a town riverside path, more a local amenity than a draw from elsewhere.

name: Collie Railway Museum
reason: Wikivoyage Collie (Museums): reconstructed railway station with railway items and the rediscovered Welsh train drawings, open 9-4 daily, by donation. Open to the public with something to see.
objection: One counted source and a small volunteer museum; a 30-minute stop only if passing through Collie.

name: Coalfields Museum
reason: Wikivoyage Collie (Museums): mining, timber, farming and social history, open 10-3 daily, $5.
objection: One counted source; a small local-history museum; Collie's coal heritage is its one distinct theme.

name: Miners Institute Collie
reason: Rule 2: an Art Deco hall (1953) Wikivoyage lists only for its exterior architecture; no public interior or tour named, so it is a civic building seen from the street.
objection: Wikivoyage's See list does single it out as 'striking'; at most a mention in Collie's description.

name: Lake Clifton
reason: Outside the region: belongs to wa-perth (the lake and its thrombolite boardwalk are in the Peel / Yalgorup National Park area; wa-perth's candidate list already has 'Lake Clifton Thrombolites').
objection: 4,446 views and a real draw (living thrombolites on a boardwalk); it must be kept in the Perth region's pass.

reason: Winery/cellar door with no counted visitor source naming it as a destination in its own right (Wikipedia winery list only; Wikivoyage Margaret River names no individual winery): fails rule 1 and the run's winery rule (a business, not a place).
objection: A board or Wikipedia winery list names it, but nothing singles it out among Margaret River's 100-plus cellar doors; the Margaret River wine region itself is the place.
